items.quote: A Secret indeed is to be concealed, it belongs onely to God to reveale it
items.note: The text says a secret is to be kept covered and that revealing it is God's alone.

items.quote: if it be disclosed, commonly it exposeth to death, or prison, or reproach, or at least to continuall fear and voluntary exilement from our friends into a far country for safety
items.note: Croll names what disclosing a secret commonly brings on the one who discloses it.

items.quote: unlesse we will brand our reputation with a perpetuall blur of lying and deceit to conceale the same
items.note: The only way named to escape those dangers is to cover the secret by lying and deceit, at the cost of one's reputation.

items.quote: Lully; Arnold, Zachary of Paris, and others, are witnesses hereof
items.name: Lully; Arnold, Zachary of Paris
items.note: Three persons are named as witnesses of what disclosure brings; the lines given report no words of theirs.

items.quote: The true Hermetick Phylosophers took an Oath that they would follow the footsteps of their fathers and masters, and not by any teinerity defile the virginity of Nature
items.note: A group is said to have sworn an oath to keep to their fathers' and masters' way and not to expose Nature.

items.quote: the virginity of Nature, which hath been preserved from the begining of the world
items.note: Nature's secrecy is spoken of in a figure, as a virginity kept from the beginning of the world.

items.quote: yet have they bequeathed their secrets to their sworn disciples who are engag'd by perpetuall faith and gratitude
items.note: The secrets are said to be handed on, but only to sworn disciples bound by faith and gratitude and made worthy by nature or education.

items.quote: which yet are with much sweat to be searched out
items.note: Even what is handed on to the disciples must still be searched out with much labour.

items.quote: Without paines-taking none is fit to injoy that Art.
items.note: The margin note says labour is the condition for enjoying 'that Art'.

items.quote: that he approveth of no sort of Physitians, but that he would professe himselfe to be the sole and onely Physitian in all the world
items.name: Men of shallow judgement
items.note: A view about Paracelsus that Croll gives to 'Men of shallow judgement' and rejects.

items.quote: whereas he only condemns the common rable of Physitians who are altogether ignorant both of Theory & Practice
items.note: Croll's own account of whom Paracelsus condemns: only the common crowd of physicians ignorant of theory and practice.

items.quote: Nor truely are they to be accounted Physitians, who Verbally and Syllogistically onely make a great flourish of Physick, but doe no cures at all
items.note: Croll denies the name of physician to those who only talk and argue physick and cure nothing.

items.quote: boasting that they have the Method of Physick
items.name: they who Verbally and Syllogistically onely make a great flourish of Physick
items.note: The boast of those verbal physicians, reported by Croll in order to reject it.

items.quote: Some of them are so incensed against that Theophrastus
items.note: In this paragraph the man called Paracelsus a few lines earlier is spoken of as 'that Theophrastus'; the lines given use both names.

items.quote: they had rather let their Patients perish then make use of his prescriptions
items.note: Croll says some physicians, out of anger at him, would sooner let patients die than use his prescriptions.

items.quote: and therefore the better they are, the more doe they undervalue them
items.note: Croll says many despise his medicines for fear their effect would blemish their own repute: the better the medicines, the more they are run down.

items.quote: falsly charge the genuine Chymists that they have lost the right method
items.name: the Censurers of Theophrastus, those fallacious Medodists
items.note: The charge made by 'the Censurers of Theophrastus, those fallacious Medodists', reported and called false.

items.quote: who linger out the cure, and lengthen the disease by their compendium
items.note: Croll's own charge against those censurers: their short way draws out the cure and lengthens the disease.

items.quote: Paracelsus observed onely that method that was agreeable to Reason and Experience
items.note: Croll's view of the method Paracelsus kept; he says it is plain to those whose understanding is enlightened.

items.quote: for without the Truth all Authority is pernicious, and all wise men will sleight it as of no value without that
items.note: Truth is set above any man's authority.

items.quote: we are not so much to regard by whom, as what it is that is spoken
items.note: What is said counts for more than who says it; no one should give up his own judgement for another's.

items.quote: True Method consisteth in the knowledg of the Disease, and the Cure of it
items.note: The text says what 'True Method' is: knowing the disease and curing it.

items.quote: what food in reason with convenient Medicines driveth away sickness, and procureth health
items.note: The same definition spelled out after 'viz.': which food, with fitting medicines, drives sickness away and brings health.

items.quote: Wimpeneus learnedly sheweth that greatest and most grievous Diseases now a dayes are in three respects cured by the Paracelsians
items.name: Wimpeneus
items.note: A named writer is given as the source of the three reasons that follow (First CH5.32, Secondly CH5.45, Thirdly CH5.46).

items.quote: First, Because the Diseases are more perfectly known
items.what: First, Because the Diseases are more perfectly known
items.note: The first of the three respects is numbered and named.

items.quote: those that sprang from Tartar cleaving to any part could not be cured, because it cannot be referred to any of those four humours
items.note: Diseases from Tartar could not be cured while all diseases were reduced to the four humours.

items.quote: And since we are here fallen upon Tartar I will speak a little more of it.
items.note: Croll announces a digression on Tartar; it runs to 'So much for Tartar.' at the end of CH5.44.

items.quote: The first Ens or Being toward life, from whence the body hath it's nourishment & food ariseth out of the last matter of the Meat by the Archaeus, or digestion of the Stomack
items.what: The first Ens or Being toward life
items.note: A thing is named and set apart: the first Ens toward life, the source of the body's nourishment, arising from the last matter of the food.

items.quote: The first Ens or Being toward life
items.note: The word 'Ens' is given with 'or Being' beside it.

items.quote: by the Archaeus, or digestion of the Stomack, it's separation, and generation of separation
items.note: Here 'the Archaeus' is given with 'or digestion of the Stomack' beside it.

items.quote: reduc'd unto Sulphur, Mercury, and Salt, as is plain in the three chief Emunctories
items.note: It is reduced to three, Sulphur, Mercury and Salt; the three chief outlets of the body are given as the evidence.

items.quote: the superfluity of Salt is separated by the Urine, that of Sulphure is divided and purged through the Entrals
items.note: How the body parts with what is too much: Salt by the urine, Sulphur through the entrails.

items.quote: Mercury or the moisture of that which nourisheth; if there be too much of it passeth through the pores by sweat
items.note: Mercury is here called the moisture of what nourishes; its excess leaves by sweat.

items.quote: Every member hath its own proper digestion, seperation, emunctory, excrement in it selfe.
items.note: The margin note gives each member its own digestion, separation, outlet and excrement.

items.quote: The first digestion of the stomack is not digestion, but apparation for the digestions of the particular members.
items.note: The note says the stomach's first digestion is not digestion but a preparing; the paragraph beside it speaks of 'the Archaeus, or digestion of the Stomack'.

items.quote: Whatsoever we eat and drink hath in it a mucilagenous, clayish, and sandy Tartar hurtful to our Health
items.note: All food and drink is said to carry a Tartar of three descriptions that harms health.

items.quote: the Stomack which is the instrument of Mans Archaeus, or the Internal, innate Chymist which God hath planted in Man
items.note: The Archaeus is called the inward, inborn Chymist planted in man by God; the stomach is its instrument.

items.quote: as soon as it taketh any thing into it self it seperateth that which is impure, dreggy, and Tartarous from the pure Nourishment
items.note: The stomach's work: on receiving anything it parts the impure and Tartarous from the pure nourishment.

items.quote: if the Stomack be strong in it's ful separative force, the pure passeth to the Members for nourishment, the impure goeth out by successe
items.note: With a strong stomach the pure goes to the members and the impure leaves the body.

items.quote: If the Stomack be weak and feeble the impure also is sent through the Mesaraick veins to the Liver, and there separated and digested the second time
items.note: With a weak stomach the impure also passes to the liver and is separated and digested there a second time.

items.quote: seperateth the pure from the impure, viz. the Rubie from the Chrystall
items.note: Two stone names are used for the pure and the impure in the liver's separation; the text goes on to say what each is.

items.quote: The Rubie is the nourishment of all the members, the heart, braine, &c.
items.note: The text says what 'the Rubie' means here.

items.quote: the Christall or that which is not the nourishment it sendeth to the reines
items.note: The text says what 'the Christall' means here: what is not nourishment, sent to the kidneys.

items.quote: this is urine, which is nothing else but the Salt pressed out of the Mercurialls, forced into resolution by the violence of separation
items.note: Urine is said to be nothing but the Salt pressed out of 'the Mercurialls'.

items.quote: If the Liver be weak and cannot well separate it sendeth it to the kidneys mucilaginous and stony
items.note: With a weak liver the matter reaches the kidneys slimy and stony.

items.quote: that is, when the spirits of Salt, viz. of the flesh and of the urine are united
items.note: The text glosses 'want of good separation' in the kidneys: the spirits of Salt of the flesh and of the urine are joined.

items.quote: the Spirit of the Salt coming between by the power of predestination, it is coagulated into Sand or Tartar, either cloddy or mucilaginous
items.note: The Spirit of the Salt is named as what thickens the matter into Sand or Tartar.

items.quote: the second which is of the stomack into haile; the third of the kidneys and bladder into a little stone
items.what: The first separation of Tartar; the second; the third
items.note: The margin note numbers three separations of Tartar and what each turns into; the first stands at a gap in the print and is said to turn into 'mosse'.

items.quote: the second which is of the stomack into haile
items.note: The note gives the stomach the second separation; the paragraph has the stomach separate first and the liver 'the second time'.

items.quote: Every Man hath mosse & haile, but not a stone in him.
items.note: The note says the first two forms are in every man, the stone not.

items.quote: Tartar therefore is the excrement of meat and drink, which by the spirit of Salt is coagulated in Man
items.note: The text says what Tartar is.

items.quote: except it be mixt together with the Excrements by the proper expulsive vertue and so cast our with them
items.note: Tartar is not coagulated in man when the body's own expelling power casts it out with the excrements.

items.quote: four kinds of Tartar, the stone of the bladder, the Sand of the Kidneys, the clods or gobbets, as also the Slime or lutous matter of the stomack
items.note: Four kinds of Tartar are counted and named by the form they take in the body.

items.quote: with many other diseases which the Ancients knew not
items.note: Croll says these and many other diseases were not known to the Ancients.

items.quote: Paracelsus distinguisheth Tartar into that which is strange or forraine proceeding from meat and drink, and that which is innate of the cruor or hereditary blood
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: A division of Tartar into two, foreign and inborn, is given to Paracelsus.

items.quote: which innate Tartarous disposition cannot be cured by the Physitian who knows not how to force Nature
items.note: The inborn Tartarous disposition is beyond the physician who cannot 'force Nature'.

items.quote: but onely by the Quint-Essence of Gold which reneweth the whole body
items.note: One remedy is named as the only cure of inborn Tartar and said to renew the whole body; the lines given do not say how it is made.

items.quote: Tartar therefore or the Naturall superfluity (the mucilage of Salt) is the mother of almost all diseases of all coagulate bodies
items.note: Tartar is given two further names, 'the Naturall superfluity' and 'the mucilage of Salt', and called the mother of almost all diseases.

items.quote: by Divine ordination, hath Poyson or a Tartarous Mucilaginous Impurity hard by or close unto the medicine or Physick thereof
items.note: In every food, by God's ordering, a poison or Tartarous impurity lies close beside its medicine.

items.quote: Paracels saith that the Matter, viz. the Tartar of diseases is twofold
items.name: Paracels
items.note: The margin note gives Paracelsus a twofold division of the Tartar of diseases, 'Bolous' and 'Viscous', each with its foods.

items.quote: Bolous, such as in milk meats, fish, and flesh
items.note: The note says which foods yield the 'Bolous' kind.

items.quote: Viscous, Bituminous, mucilaginous such is the excrement of pulse, coleworts, roots, fruits, &c.
items.note: The note says which foods yield the 'Viscous' kind.

items.quote: There are four sorts of Tartar, springing from the fourfold fruits of the Elements by which we are nourished.
items.note: Four sorts of Tartar are announced, by the fourfold fruits of the Elements; CH5.39-42 number them.

items.quote: There are four sorts of Tartar, springing from the fourfold fruits of the Elements
items.note: This four is counted by the source of the food; the 'four kinds of Tartar' of CH5.35 are counted by the form in the body (stone, sand, clods, slime). The lines given do not say how the two fours relate.

items.quote: The first sort ariseth from the use of those things which grow in the Earth, as Pulse of all sorts, Hearbs, &c. upon which we feed.
items.note: First sort: from what grows in the Earth.

items.quote: The second cometh from the nourishment which we have from the Water, as Fish, shell-Fish.
items.note: Second sort: from the Water.

items.quote: The third is in the Flesh of Beasts and Fowles.
items.note: Third sort: in the flesh of beasts and fowls; no element is named in this line.

items.quote: The fourth from the Firmament, which is most like to the Spirit of wine in its subtilty, and hath the strongest impression of all
items.note: Fourth sort: from the Firmament, likened to Spirit of wine for fineness and said to press strongest.

items.quote: if the Aire be infected by the vapours of the Earth, and Water, and Firmament, afterward it affecteth us also
items.note: The air, infected by vapours of Earth, Water and Firmament, then affects men.

items.quote: those acute and pernicious Astrall diseases, the Pleuresie, Plague
items.note: A class of diseases is named 'Astrall' and examples given.

items.quote: which diseases proceeding from the impressions of the Stars the universall medicine powerfull expelleth
items.note: A thing is named 'the universall medicine' and said to drive out the diseases that come from the impressions of the Stars; the lines given do not say what it is.

items.quote: Those four kinds of Tartar shew themselves in the Urine, and are judged of by the art of separation
items.note: The kind of Tartar behind a disease is found in the urine by 'the art of separation'.

items.quote: He that knoweth what sort of food any one eateth, may also know his disease, or he that knoweth the disease may know what he eateth
items.note: Food and disease are said to be knowable one from the other.

items.quote: The disease is cured by the same Element that was the cause of it.
items.note: A rule of cure: by the same Element that caused the disease.

items.quote: which Paracelsus comprehendeth under the name of Poyson and Tartar
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: The excrements of meat and drink are what Paracelsus is said to mean by the names 'Poyson' and 'Tartar'.

items.quote: Choller and Melancholly had long since been rooted out of the Physitians Garden
items.note: Croll says that with true knowledge of these excrements Galen and his followers would long ago have given up Choler and Melancholy; said in the figure of a garden.

items.quote: cannot possibly understand how the Author of diseases afflicteth us, by destroying the frame of the little world and taking away our life
items.note: Without knowing the Tartarous matter one cannot understand how 'the Author of diseases' afflicts man; man is here 'the little world'.

items.quote: viz. our Naturall Heat, or the microcosmicall heat of the Sun and Moon that is in us, whereby the Nutriment is digested
items.note: What breaks the spirit of coagulation and parts Tartar from nourishment is named: our natural heat, also called the microcosmical heat of the Sun and Moon in us.

items.quote: the microcosmicall heat of the Sun and Moon that is in us
items.note: 'Sun and Moon' are here spoken of as within man, not as the lights of the sky.

items.quote: then it must be strengthned by its like, that is, by the macrocosmicall Heat of Sun and Moon, if it could be got
items.note: When the separating power is weakened, the inner heat must be strengthened by its like, the heat of Sun and Moon of the great world; 'if it could be got' marks it as hard to come by.

items.quote: even the most simple matter which the most Great God generated of the spirit of the world (one and the same with the spirit of our body) for the restauration and conservation of Humane Nature
items.note: That macrocosmical heat is named again as one 'most simple matter' made by God from the spirit of the world for restoring and keeping human nature; the lines given do not name it further.

items.quote: the spirit of the world (one and the same with the spirit of our body)
items.note: The spirit of the world and the spirit of man's body are said to be one and the same.

items.quote: and is deduced by art into act, viz. turned into such a simple spirit as is the spirit of our life, which is done by resolution and conjuction with the Nutriment
items.note: The other way named: things holding the power of Sun and Moon are brought 'by art into act', turned into a simple spirit like the spirit of life, by resolution and joining with the nutriment.

items.quote: The Vitall spirit in Man and the Elementall is but one spirit.
items.note: The margin note states the oneness of the vital spirit in man and the elemental spirit.

items.quote: then the excrements stay in the Chylus, and cause stomachall diseases in the stomack, Jecorall in the liver
items.note: If the Archaeus of stomach, liver or kidneys is infected or hindered, the excrements stay in the Chylus and cause the diseases of each place.

items.quote: and breed the Gout in the hands, feet, knees, from congelation of the glew by the spirit of Salt
items.note: The Gout is said to come from the stiffening of 'the glew' by the spirit of Salt.

items.quote: Tartar differeth according to the places of the bodies pores and passages
items.note: The margin note says Tartar differs by its place in the body and lists the places.

items.quote: Therefore the Archaeus of the stomack must destroy the Tartar of the Elements least it be turned into the Tartar of Man
items.what: the Tartar of the Elements; the Tartar of Man
items.note: Two Tartars are set apart by name: 'the Tartar of the Elements' and 'the Tartar of Man'.

items.quote: the spirit of the Sun which is Lord and Master of coagulation in various subjects will breed the Stone
items.note: Here the spirit of the Sun is lord of coagulation and breeds the Stone; CH5.35 has Tartar coagulated in man 'by the spirit of Salt'. The lines given do not say how the two relate.

items.quote: So much for Tartar.
items.note: Closes the digression on Tartar opened at the end of CH5.32.

items.quote: Secondly, Because we have more perfect medicines now then heretofore, that is to say, of Mineralls
items.what: Secondly, Because we have more perfect medicines now then heretofore
items.note: The second of the three respects: more perfect medicines, namely of minerals.

items.quote: whose preparations and due administrations were discovered to those skilfull Chymists the Sons of Cadmus
items.note: The Chymists to whom the preparing and giving of mineral medicines was 'discovered' are named 'the Sons of Cadmus'; the lines given do not say why.

items.quote: A knotty piece must be cloven with hard wedges
items.note: A saying about wood is used for diseases and remedies; the paragraph ends by saying its sense plainly: extreme diseases call for extreme remedies.

items.quote: Paracelsus would have a steely medicine applied as proper for an iron disease, for extream diseases call for extream remedies
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: A rule of cure given to Paracelsus, in the figure of steel against iron.

items.quote: Thirdly, Because now the Harmony between the great and little world is made so plaine, and so well understood
items.what: Thirdly, Because now the Harmony between the great and little world is made so plaine
items.note: The third respect: the harmony of the great and the little world is now plainly understood.

items.quote: as Silver, Saphir, Vitrioll, Emeralds, for the braine; for the heart, Gold, Pearles, Saffron; for the lungs, Brimstone, &c.
items.note: From that harmony it is said to be easy to know which medicine is 'familiar and friendly' to which member; three members are given with their medicines.

items.quote: Whereas Paracelsus offendeth Galen, Galen did the same to others
items.note: Croll answers the reproach that Paracelsus goes against Galen: Galen went against others too.

items.quote: Hippocrates wrote many things, which most Galenists reject at this day
items.note: Most Galenists are said to reject much of what Hippocrates wrote.

items.quote: nor doe the stoutest of common vulgar Physitians agree among themselves
items.note: The common physicians do not agree with one another.

items.quote: by those that differ in their most pugnacious opinions, and that are ignorant Mechanick forgers of diseases
items.note: Croll's words for the disputing physicians.

items.quote: As between Schekius and Fuchsius about the continent Cause of diseases.
items.note: First of five disputes named as examples: two persons and their matter of dispute; no words of theirs are reported.

items.quote: You may find more jarring in opinions in Agryppa
items.name: Agryppa
items.note: The margin note sends the reader to a named writer's chapter on medicine for more such disagreements; part of the title stands at a gap.

items.quote: Between Argenterius and Fernelius about Agues and Fevers.
items.note: Second dispute named.

items.quote: Between Galen and Rondeletius concerning the Palsie, Epilepsie and Stone.
items.note: Third dispute named.

items.quote: Between Francaneianus, Rondelatius and Fallopius about the French Pox.
items.note: Fourth dispute named; the second name is spelled 'Rondelatius' here and 'Rondeletius' in the sentence before.

items.quote: Between Altomarus and Fernelius concerning the Gout.
items.note: Fifth dispute named.

items.quote: How many millions, according to the disagreeing and jarring method of these men, will still perish, before the genuine cause of the said diseases be determined
items.note: Croll says many will die before these physicians settle the cause of the diseases they dispute.

items.quote: Here for brevity sake I willingly passe by the Herbarists, who commonly squabble and raile at one another with endlesse jangling about the Wool of Plants
items.note: Croll says he passes over the Herbarists and their quarrels for shortness.

items.quote: Therefore I exhort and admonish all Students of Hippocraticall and Galenicall Physick, in whom the Philosophicall veine is yet warme
items.what: I exhort and admonish all Students of Hippocraticall and Galenicall Physick
items.note: Croll names whom he addresses and announces an exhortation.

items.quote: know that what our industry hath found out should not shut the door against that of the Ancients, as if all the strength of Nature were hatched in us onely
items.note: The students he addresses are those who hold that new findings should not shut out the Ancients'.

items.quote: that they would forsake their Fathers faults and other mens errours
items.note: First thing urged: to leave inherited faults and others' errors.

items.quote: that they would also spend some time in reading the works of this new Phylosopher and Physitian, not superficially and prefunctorily, but with greatest diligence and attention of mind
items.note: Second thing urged: to read the works of 'this new Phylosopher and Physitian' with the greatest care.

items.quote: we are to imitate the experience and industry of the Bees, who suck and gather their hony out of the most fragrant juice of the flowers, segregating the best from the worst
items.note: The way to read is given in a figure: as bees gather, taking the best and leaving the worst.

items.quote: I doe not so far perswade men that they should so adore every thing of Paracelsus
items.note: Croll limits his own exhortation: not everything of Paracelsus is to be adored as if it were 'Gospel-Oracles'.

items.quote: inasmuch as he himselfe hath recanted something of his over hasty writings
items.note: Croll says Paracelsus himself took back some of what he wrote too hastily.

items.quote: as we see many who even worship the conclusions, and opinions of Hethen Authors
items.note: Croll sets beside this the many who worship the opinions of heathen authors.

items.quote: the diligent and accurate reading of him may give us greater light, and be no small advantage to us for the more intimate and right understanding of Hippocrates his works
items.note: The reason given for reading Paracelsus: more light, and a better understanding of Hippocrates' works.

items.quote: They are not to be praised who rashly condemn all that Paracelsus hath written, when yet they have not read so much as his marginall notes
items.note: Croll blames those who condemn all of Paracelsus without having read even his margin notes.

items.quote: or if they have, yet truly they understand not fully the third part of them
items.note: And those who have read them are said not to understand a third of them.

items.quote: who throw away the kernell and pick up onely the husks of Phylosophers
items.note: Those addressed as 'Phylosopasters' are said to keep the husk and throw away the kernel: an outer and an inner part of the philosophers' writings.

items.quote: pray to God, and seek to Books of Paper, for the spirit, that ye may understand the dead letter of Theophrastus, and the Phylosophers
items.note: The letter of Theophrastus and the philosophers is called dead; understanding it needs 'the spirit', to be asked of God.

items.quote: His works which were Printed for the publick good, by the incouragement and at the cost of that most Renowned and Reverend Ernestus Prince Elector of Coleine
items.what: His works which were Printed for the publick good
items.note: The printing of Paracelsus' works is named, with the prince said to have encouraged and paid for it.

items.quote: have given occasion to his adversaries to charge him with implicite and evident contradiction
items.name: his adversaries
items.note: The charge of contradiction is given to Paracelsus' adversaries; Croll goes on to give the cause in his manner of writing.

items.quote: because to the unskilfull and unlearned he wrote in a Magicall stile
items.note: The cause given for the seeming contradiction: he wrote in a 'Magicall stile'.

items.quote: not for the vulgar sort, but for himselfe and the understanding children of Wisdome trained up in the School of Magick
items.note: For whom he is said to have written: himself and the 'children of Wisdome', not the common sort.

items.quote: not for the Sophisticall Alchymists, such as are bewitch'd with a greedy desire of Gold
items.note: A second group shut out: the 'Sophisticall Alchymists' greedy for gold.

items.quote: incensed with a righteous hatred against some most wretched, wicked, inhumane Physitians and Druggists of his time, who often lay in wait to poyson him to the shortning of his life
items.note: A motive given for his manner of writing: hatred, called righteous, of physicians and druggists who sought to poison him.

items.quote: those circumforanceous and vulgar Alchymists would have surpassed all other Physitians, and prostituted the Art to the great wrong and injury of Nature
items.note: What plainer writing would have brought, as Croll gives it: the vulgar Alchymists would have outdone all physicians and made the Art common.

items.quote: He concealed his mysteries under vulgar and various names
items.note: Paracelsus is said to have hidden his mysteries under common and changing names.

items.quote: therefore we must not take the similitudes for the truth it selfe, or that which is intended by them
items.note: A rule of reading: his likenesses are not the thing meant by them.

items.quote: the Physicall Secrets, that is, the hidden power of God, or the Magicall WORDS in Paracelsus
items.note: The text says what 'the Physicall Secrets' are: the hidden power of God, or the Magicall WORDS in Paracelsus.

items.quote: they need and require a Delian swimmer, a most acute and sharp wit, a Magicall Understanding, even that purified eye of the Mind
items.note: What the reader needs to search out the hidden sentences: named in four ways, the last 'that purified eye of the Mind'.

items.quote: I mean that which is True and lawfull
items.note: Croll says what he means by Magick, and that he means it so everywhere; the word itself stands at a gap in the print.

items.quote: or wichcraft, which is fit for none but Vulcan, and deserveth to be burned
items.note: What he does not mean by it: the infamous and profane kind (a word in foreign script, not given) or witchcraft, fit for the fire.

items.quote: the absolute perfection of the whole most noble Phylosophy, the chiefest Wisdome of Gods works and the plenary knowledge of occult Nature
items.note: The definition itself: the perfection of philosophy, the chief wisdom of God's works, the full knowledge of hidden Nature.

items.quote: doth things exceeding the usuall order of Nature, by a fit application of Agents and Patients, observing the consent and dissent of things
items.note: How it works its wonders: by fitly applying agents to patients and keeping to the agreement and disagreement of things.

items.quote: Paracelsus hath joyned the exercetation of either medicine together, as well that of Physick as of Chyrurgie, in imitation and after the example of Great Hippocrates
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: Paracelsus is said to have joined physick and surgery, following Hippocrates.

items.quote: a twofold Medicine, Physicall or the knowledge of all diseases, and Chyrurgicall or the curing of the same
items.note: The two medicines are defined: 'Physicall' is the knowing of diseases, 'Chyrurgicall' the curing of them.

items.quote: Nor can either without the other safely consist or be exercised but with great hurt and danger of the sick
items.note: Neither can be practised without the other without danger to the sick.

items.quote: it is necessary that every Surgeon should be a Physician, and every Physitian a Chyrurgion, that there may be a sound Bridgroom for a sound Bride
items.note: The joining of the two in one man is put in the figure of bridegroom and bride.

items.quote: their preparations and compositions made by the Physitian himselfe, and not carelesly left to others
items.note: The physician himself must choose, prepare and compound the medicines.

items.quote: by their own hand to prepare the medicaments which they know, to seperate and purge them from their poyson and dreggs, to reduce them to their pure simplicity
items.note: The work that marks the 'genuine Physitian': with his own hand to prepare the medicines, part them from poison and dregs, and bring them to pure simplicity.

items.quote: For the Bad and Good are mixt together, neither is Sugar free from faeculent impurity, nor is honey voyd of a venemous bitternesse
items.note: The reason given: good and bad are mixed in things, even in sugar and honey.

items.quote: he must with true faith and acurate skill or judgement accommodate them to mans necessities, that the root of the disease may be plucked up
items.note: After preparing, the medicines are to be fitted to the patient's need so that the root of the disease is removed.

items.quote: he must both know and prepare his medicines, for judgement without practice is altogether barren and fruitlesse
items.note: A physician needs theory and practice together; judgement without practice bears nothing.

items.quote: Physick is learned by the labour of the hands and practicall working or making it up, when the Fire discovereth new and most pleasant Remedies continually
items.note: Physick is learned by handwork, and the Fire is said to uncover new remedies continually.

items.quote: which Nature dayly more and more purgeth from their superfluities, and then delivereth them to her Servant to make them up
items.note: Nature is said to cleanse the remedies and hand them to 'her Servant' to make up.

items.quote: will not become schollers and school-boyes againe, to dig they are ashamed
items.note: The great Doctors grown grey in common physick will not learn again.

items.quote: so these men will openly contradict the truth, and with a canine obstinate bawling bark at it
items.note: Croll likens them to an old tree and an old dog: they oppose the truth rather than mend their errors.

items.quote: they exclaime and cry out against the Chymists as if they were no Physitians
items.name: these Rationall Physitians
items.note: The charge of the 'Rationall Physitians' against the Chymists, reported by Croll, who adds that the Chymists are the most skilful of any.

items.quote: that they are the onely Physitians who in judgement and Reason (undervaluing Chymistry) know how to apply any Remedy to every disease
items.name: these Rationall Physitians
items.note: Their claim for themselves, reported in order to be rejected.

items.quote: because they can prepare their medicines but onely with their Reason, not at all with their hand
items.note: Croll's reason why they stand helpless at the sick bed: they prepare with reason only, not with the hand.

items.quote: Yet here I will by no means undertake to defend them, who reteining the works of Hippocrates and of the Ancients, yet boast themselves to be the Schollers of Paracelsus
items.note: Croll refuses to defend those who keep the Ancients and yet call themselves scholars of Paracelsus.

items.quote: but neither acknowledge the minde of the Author in his Theory, nor doe any thing praise-worthy in Practice
items.note: His charge against them: they grasp neither his theory nor achieve anything in practice.

items.quote: These Receits being lost by chance, all the Wisdome vanisheth from them
items.note: The margin note says their wisdom lies in recipes and is gone when these are lost.

items.quote: Experience, without Phylosophy the mother of Experience is uncertaine.
items.note: The note calls Phylosophy the mother of Experience and experience without it uncertain.

items.quote: There are also false and lying Theophrasteans prophaning by their avarice and timerity that Divine Physick
items.note: A further group is named and set apart: false 'Theophrasteans' who profane 'that Divine Physick'.

items.quote: who under disguised names vaunt and vapour that they make use of Theophrastus his medicines
items.note: They are said to boast, under disguised names, of using Theophrastus' medicines.

items.quote: being altogether ignorant not onely of Phylosophicall, but even of vulgar and common medicines
items.note: They are said to know neither the philosophical nor even the common medicines.

items.quote: who disdaining the writings of the Ancients
items.note: They are blamed for scorning the writings of the Ancients.

items.quote: These men get their knowledge piece-meale out of men, & gaine their experience by the death of others
items.note: The margin note says how such men come by their knowledge and experience.

items.quote: I know not what Secrets and Experiences they trust to
items.note: Croll says he does not know what 'Secrets and Experiences' they rely on.

items.quote: they doubt not to attempt and take in hand the cure of greatest and most dangerous diseases before they scarce know how to put fire into the furnace
items.note: They undertake the gravest cures before they can so much as fire a furnace.

items.quote: or else cure the party and his disease at once with a turse of the Church-yard
items.note: 'Cure' is not meant plainly here: patient and disease are 'cured' together with something of the church-yard.

items.quote: all the Medicines both of the Arabians and Grecians, are desperate and without hope of doing any good, and so become laughing-stocks to the disease
items.note: Croll grants that in great diseases the medicines of the Arabians and Grecians sometimes fail altogether.

items.quote: many times the cure is left to the absurd Remedies of Old Wives and Empericks to the great dishonour and ignominy of Physitians
items.note: The cure is then often left to old wives and Empericks, to the physicians' shame.

items.quote: these circumforaneous and adulterous Theophrasteans, with their unlawfully prepared Remedies
items.note: The false Theophrasteans are named again, with remedies called unlawfully prepared.

items.quote: No rabble of Physitians in the City is more numerous then these.
items.note: The margin note says no crowd of physicians in the City is larger than these.

items.quote: doe sometime exceed many Galenists in many great and perilous diseases
items.note: Croll grants that these men sometimes do better than many Galenists.

items.quote: yet no conscientious man will ever approve their uncertaine, bold, rash, dangerous, impious practice of Physick
items.note: Even so their practice is not to be approved; it endangers the sick by doubtful experiments.
